The application is emotional text-to-speech (TTS) / speech synthesis, which is within the audio domain.
The paper is an original method with experiments and a conclusion, not a survey or review article.
evidence_highlights: "we turn to preference learning to further refine its performance"
"For Emo-DPO training, we create pairwise preference data ... as preferred ... and other emotion audio ... as dis-preferred"
"Controllable emotional speech synthesis through direct preference optimization"
"Current emotional text-to-speech (TTS) models"
decision_rationale: The title, abstract, and full text directly support all Stage 2 inclusion criteria: the work is a preference-learning method, it is applied to audio via emotional TTS/speech synthesis, and it is not a survey or review. The paper also uses pairwise preferred vs. dis-preferred audio examples in training, so the preference signal is part of learning rather than evaluation only. No exclusion criterion is triggered.

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text states that the model is fit to a large dataset of crowdsourced human judgments in audio.
The paper explicitly uses pairwise comparison on two audio recordings: subjects answer whether two recordings are the same or different.
The learned metric is used for training, not just evaluation: "simply replacing an existing loss ... with our metric" improves a denoising network.
The paper includes audio-domain A/B preference tests and subjective pairwise comparison experiments.
evidence_highlights: "we construct a metric by fitting a deep neural network to a new large dataset of crowdsourced human judgments"
"We present a listener with two recordings ... and ask if these two recordings are exactly same or different"
"we train a neural network with this data, and use the learned representation to construct a distance metric"
"simply replacing an existing loss ... with our metric yields significant improvement in a denoising network"
"We perform A/B preference tests on AMT"
decision_rationale: This is an original audio-domain learning paper that uses binary pairwise judgments on two recordings to train a perceptual metric and then applies that learned metric as a loss in speech enhancement. That satisfies the Stage 2 preference/comparison and learning requirements, and the full text does not indicate a survey or review article.
